chunks: "Stability means the output regulates to a steady value and any disturbance, like a load step or noise, dies out instead of growing or ringing forever.
Mathematically, for the small-signal model, the closed-loop poles are all in the left half-plane.
A buck is a feedback system: I divide down the output, compare it to a reference, run it through a compensator and use that to set the duty cycle.
At low frequency the feedback is negative, which is what regulates.
The problem is that the power stage has an LC filter, which adds up to 180 degrees of phase lag around its resonance, and the compensator, delay and sampling add more.
If the loop still has gain above one when the total lag reaches 180 degrees, the feedback becomes positive and the loop oscillates. So I look at the loop gain on a Bode plot.
Where the gain crosses 0 decibels, the phase margin tells me how far I am from minus 180, and I want about 45 to 60 degrees.
The gain margin tells me how much the gain could rise before it breaks, and I want 6 to 10 decibels or more.
A good phase margin gives a well damped step response, while a low margin gives ringing and overshoot, and zero margin gives sustained oscillation.
There are other instabilities too, like subharmonic oscillation in peak current mode, but the loop-gain picture is what people usually mean."
